related-article.article-title: Erratum: Phase I Study of Telisotuzumab Adizutecan (Temab-A, ABBV-400), a Novel c-Met Antibody-Drug Conjugate, in Patients With Late-Line Colorectal Cancer and Advanced Solid Tumors
Has Colorectal Cancer (c-)Met Its Match With Telisotuzumab Adizutecan?

sec.title: PURPOSE
sec.p: The antibody-drug conjugate Temab-A comprises the c-Met–targeting antibody telisotuzumab conjugated to a novel topoisomerase 1 inhibitor payload, adizutecan. A first-in-human phase I study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05029882) of Temab-A in patients with advanced solid tumors whose disease has progressed is currently ongoing. We report results from all patients in the dose escalation and the monotherapy metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) dose expansion.

sec.title: METHODS
sec.p: Temab-A was administered intravenously once every 3 weeks as a monotherapy starting at 1.6 mg/kg in dose escalation. In mCRC dose expansion, patients with confirmed BRAF wild-type, microsatellite stable/mismatch repair-proficient mCRC were randomly assigned to 1.6 mg/kg, 2.4 mg/kg, or 3.0 mg/kg Temab-A once every 3 weeks. Primary end points included safety, pharmacokinetics, recommended phase II dose of Temab-A monotherapy, and Temab-A efficacy in patients with mCRC.

sec.title: RESULTS
sec.p: In total, 57 patients received ≥1 dose of Temab-A in dose escalation; 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks was established as the maximum tolerated dose. Collectively, in dose escalation and dose expansion, 122 patients with mCRC received Temab-A (dose escalation, N = 29; randomized dose optimization expansion, N = 93). All patients experienced ≥1 treatment-emergent adverse event; the most frequent were gastrointestinal (78%) and hematologic (71%) toxicities. Treatment-related discontinuations and deaths were infrequent (10% and 3%, respectively). Across all doses in patients with mCRC, overall response rate was 15.6% (95% CI, 9.6 to 23.2), disease control rate was 74.6% (95% CI, 65.9 to 82.0), and duration of response was 5.9 months (95% CI, 4.1 to 10.5); responses were more frequent at doses of 2.4 mg/kg and 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks. Median progression-free survival was 4.6 months (95% CI: 4.0, 5.4), and median overall survival was 10.4 months (95% CI, 8.9 to 13.1).

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: Temab-A at 2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks has a tolerable and manageable safety profile, with promising antitumor activity.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Increased c-Met (MET) protein expression has been reported in various cancers, including metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC),1 gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma (GEA),2 and non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).3 In mCRC, increased c-Met protein has been observed in approximately 50%-70% of cases.4,5 Mechanistically, c-Met protein activation promotes tumor cell proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, invasion, and metastasis, thereby contributing to more aggressive disease behavior and reduced survival.4-6 Indeed, meta-analysis and large cohort studies confirm that increased c-Met protein expression is a significant predictor of poor overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) in mCRC.4,6

list-item.p: To evaluate the safety of Temab-A in patients with solid tumors and assess the efficacy of Temab-A in patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC).

Temab-A monotherapy demonstrated manageable safety and promising antitumor activity in patients with solid tumors, including those with mCRC, where overall response rates were enriched in patients with increased c-Met expression. The enriched responses observed among patients with increased c-Met protein expression validate c-Met protein as a target in patients with third-line CRC and the promising efficacy data suggest that Temab-A may represent an important addition to the mCRC treatment landscape in the future.

Initial data support target density and dose as factors associated with response for this MET-directed antibody-drug conjugate (ADC), which will require confirmation in future studies. The role of telisotuzumab adizutecan versus other topo 1–based ADCs will also be an important question.*
*Relevance section written by JCO Associate Editor Robert G. Maki, MD, PhD, FACP, FASCO.

sec.p: Advancements in the treatment of mCRC have led to improved outcomes, although survival for patients remains dismal (5-year survival rate of 14%).7 For patients with unresectable mCRC that is microsatellite stable or mismatch repair-proficient, BRAF V600E wild-type, and has progressed after fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin, and irinotecan, third-line standard-of-care (SOC) options are limited. Current treatments include trifluridine/tipiracil with or without bevacizumab, regorafenib, and the recently approved fruquintinib. Among these, the combination of trifluridine/tipiracil and bevacizumab has emerged as the most commonly used regimen, representing a significant advancement in the third-line setting, with median progression-free survival (mPFS) of 5.6 months and median overall survival (mOS) of 10.8 months reported.8 Fruquintinib monotherapy has also demonstrated clinical benefit, with mPFS and mOS of 3.7 and 7.4 months, respectively.9 However, there remains a need to improve response rates and survival without negatively affecting safety and quality of life, particularly in those patients with mCRC.

Temab-A is an ADC comprising the c-Met–targeting antibody telisotuzumab (ABT-700) conjugated to a novel potent topoisomerase 1 (Top1) inhibitor payload, adizutecan, with a drug-antibody ratio of 6.10,11 Temab-A has demonstrated favorable pharmacokinetics, antiproliferative action in vitro, and potent antitumor activity in models of mCRC, NSCLC, and GEA.12 An ongoing phase I first-in-human, multipart trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05029882) is evaluating Temab-A in patients with solid tumors whose disease has progressed on standard therapies.13-15 We report results from the monotherapy dose escalation and the dose expansion in patients with mCRC.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: This is a phase I, open-label, multicenter study evaluating Temab-A in patients with solid tumors, including mCRC. The study comprised a dose escalation of Temab-A monotherapy in patients with advanced solid tumors, a monotherapy dose expansion of Temab-A in various indications, including NSCLC, GEA, mCRC, MET-amplified, and MET-mutant advanced solid tumors, and a combination arm evaluating Temab-A plus bevacizumab in patients with mCRC (Appendix Fig A1, online only). We report on dose escalation in all patients (part 1) and on dose expansion in patients with mCRC (part 4). Temab-A was administered intravenously (IV) once every 3 weeks until disease progression, intolerable toxicity, or consent withdrawal. In dose escalation, patients received escalating doses of IV Temab-A (initial dose of 1.6 mg/kg once every 3 weeks). The planned doses in dose escalation portion were sequentially tested, and dose escalations/de-escalations were guided by the Bayesian optimal interval (BOIN) design16 with a target toxicity rate of 30%; dose-escalation decisions were based on prespecified observed dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) rate boundaries. A minimum of 3 DLT-evaluable patients were required per dose level and at least 6 DLT-evaluable patients were required to declare the maximum tolerated dose (MTD). The MTD was defined as the highest dose level at which the observed DLT rate did not exceed the BOIN de-escalation boundary (≤33.3%). In total, 57 patients were enrolled in Part 1 dose escalation, including backfilling. DLTs were assessed during the first cycle, with each cycle being 21 days. DLTs included grade ≥2 interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis, most grade ≥3 nonhematologic toxicities (with protocol-specified exceptions for short-lived or controlled events), grade 4 hematologic toxicities (except transient neutropenia, leukopenia, or lymphopenia lasting ≤7 days), significant hepatic or renal laboratory abnormalities, any treatment-related toxicity resulting in >7-day delay of cycle 2, and any treatment-related death. In the mCRC dose expansion phase, patients received IV Temab-A monotherapy once every 3 weeks at doses of 1.6 mg/kg, 2.4 mg/kg, or 3.0 mg/kg to support dose optimization and establish the recommended phase II dose (RP2D). Randomization was centrally managed, beginning with a 1:1 allocation between the 2.4 mg/kg and 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks cohorts. After the addition of the 1.6 mg/kg once every 3 weeks cohort, randomization was adjusted to a 1:1:5 ratio to maintain similar enrollment across all dose levels. No stratification factors were used.

The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines of the International Conference on Harmonisation and approved by regulatory and independent ethics committees/institutional review boards at each site. All patients provided written informed consent before any study procedures were performed.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Patients age 18 years and older with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status ≤1 and measurable disease per RECIST v1.117 were eligible. Dose escalation enrolled patients with advanced solid tumors whose disease had progressed on SOC therapies and was not amenable to surgical resection or other approved therapies with clinical benefit. For dose expansion, patients with mCRC (confirmed by pathology and/or cytology) that did not harbor the BRAF V600E mutation and were not mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability high with progression on a fluoropyrimidine, oxaliplatin, irinotecan, and, if applicable, anti–epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), anti–vascular endothelial growth factor monoclonal antibody, or targeted therapy were enrolled. Patients ineligible for or who experienced intolerance to standard therapy and those who received prior trifluridine/tipiracil or regorafenib were also eligible. Patients with a history of (1) ILD or pneumonitis that required treatment with systemic steroids or (2) idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, organizing pneumonia, drug-induced pneumonitis, or idiopathic pneumonitis were excluded. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria are detailed in the Protocol (online only).

sec.title: Outcomes and Assessments
sec.p: Primary end points were safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics (PK), RP2D of Temab-A monotherapy, and Temab-A efficacy in patients with mCRC. Adverse event (AE) terms are as reported by the investigative site according to Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities preferred term. The primary efficacy end point was confirmed overall response rate (ORR; complete response [CR]/partial response [PR] per RECIST v1.1 as assessed by investigator). Secondary efficacy end points were duration of response (DOR) for patients with confirmed CR/PR, PFS, and OS. DOR was defined as the time from initial CR/PR to disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. Disease control rate was defined as the percentage of patients who had CR, PR, or stable disease. Tumor assessments were performed at baseline and approximately every 6 weeks, increasing to every 12 weeks after 1 year, until radiographic progression, initiation of new anticancer treatment, death, or withdrawn consent. PK end points included maximum observed serum (or plasma for payload) concentration (Cmax), time to reach Cmax, terminal phase elimination half-life, area under the serum (or plasma for payload) concentration versus time curve for conjugate, total antibody, and unconjugated Top1 inhibitor payload. Blood samples were collected on day 1 of each cycle and on days 2, 3, 8, and 15 of cycles 1 and 3. PK parameters were determined using noncompartmental methods for conjugate, total antibody, and unconjugated Top1 inhibitor payload.

Midway through the study, a risk mitigation plan for ILD was implemented; this involved exclusion of patients with clinically significant, intercurrent lung-specific illnesses and establishment of an independent ILD adjudication committee that retrospectively reviewed suspected cases of ILD. These precautions were incorporated due to the known risk of ILD/pneumonitis associated with ADCs and to ensure patient safety.

sec.title: Biomarker Analysis
sec.p: c-Met protein expression was retrospectively evaluated by immunohistochemistry (IHC; clinical trial assay for MET [SP44], Roche Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN) using formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor samples from archival or recently obtained (within 6 months) tissue. Cytomembrane staining intensity and the percentage of c-Met protein–positive tumor cells were assessed, and their association with clinical response to Temab-A treatment was evaluated. c-Met protein positivity was defined as ≥10% of tumor cells exhibiting 3+ staining intensity (≥10%|3+), consistent with criteria used in prior biomarker studies evaluating c-Met protein expression by IHC as a predictive biomarker.6,18

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: The full analysis set included all patients with mCRC who received ≥1 dose of Temab-A and was used for safety, efficacy, PK, and baseline analyses. This included the two patients who were enrolled in backfill after dose escalation completion and not included in dose escalation analyses. ORR was summarized with the 2-sided 95% exact CI based on the Clopper-Pearson (exact) method.19 Time-to-event end points were summarized by Kaplan-Meier estimates, with the median calculated with 2-sided 95% CIs.

sec.title: Dose Escalation in Patients With Solid Tumors
sec.p: In total, 57 patients enrolled and received ≥1 dose of Temab-A (1.6 mg/kg once every 3 weeks, n = 3; 2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks, n = 16; 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks, n = 18; 3.5 mg/kg once every 3 weeks, n = 6; 4.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks, n = 9; 6.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks, n = 5; data cutoff: August 23, 2024). Patient demographics and baseline disease characteristics are presented in Appendix Table A1. Median age was 58 years (range, 34–79), 54% of patients were male, and the most common primary tumors were mCRC (47%) and GEA (14%). Median follow-up was 19.2 months. Median treatment duration was 4.3 months (range, 0.7-31.5), with a median relative dose intensity of 84%; relative dose intensity generally decreased with increasing dose (100% at 1.6 mg/kg once every 3 weeks v 40% at 6.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks).

All patients experienced ≥1 treatment-emergent AE (TEAE; Appendix Table A2); most common TEAEs were anemia (37; 65%), nausea (32; 56%), and fatigue (30; 53%). Grade ≥3 TEAEs were experienced by 83% of patients; hematologic events were the most common (74%) and were dose- and exposure-dependent. During dose escalation, 18 DLTs occurred in 13 patients (23%); all occurred in dose cohorts ≥3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks (Appendix Table A3). The 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks dose was subsequently established as the MTD of Temab-A monotherapy, as more than 33.3% of DLTs were observed at all doses ≥3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks. Efficacy outcomes are reported in Appendix Table A4.

sec.title: Dose Escalation and Expansion in Patients With mCRC
sec.p: A total of 122 patients with mCRC were enrolled and had received ≥1 dose of Temab-A monotherapy across the dose escalation (N = 29) and randomized dose optimization expansion (N = 93; Appendix Fig A1). Patient demographics and baseline disease characteristics are shown in Table 1. Median age was 56 years (range, 24-81), 53% were male, 67% had liver metastasis, and of those with known mutation status, 55% had KRAS mutations and 15% had NRAS mutations. Median number of prior lines of systemic therapies was 4.0 (range, 1-12); 92% had received prior bevacizumab, 39% received prior anti-EGFR therapy, 31% received prior trifluridine/tipiracil, and 95% had received a Top1 inhibitor (eg, irinotecan). Median follow-up was 13.1 months; median treatment duration was 4.1 months (range, 0.7-18.1), with a relative dose intensity of 95.1%. A higher relative dose intensity was observed at doses of 1.6 and 2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks versus the MTD of 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks (99.6% and 95.7% v 86.5%, respectively). Patient disposition is displayed in Appendix Table A5.

sec.p: Safety data are presented in Table 2. All patients experienced ≥1 TEAE and 74% experienced a grade ≥3 TEAE; most frequent events were GI (78%) and hematologic (71%) toxicities. The most common hematologic any-grade TEAEs were anemia (58%), neutropenia (43%), leukopenia (28%), and thrombocytopenia (25%), with the majority being grade 1/2. The most frequent grade ≥3 hematologic TEAEs were anemia (38%) and neutropenia (28%). Of 58% of patients who reported ≥1 event of anemia, dose reductions and interruptions were noted in 11% and 17% of patients, respectively. Of the 43% of patients who reported ≥1 event of neutropenia, dose reductions and interruptions were required in 8% and 22% of patients, respectively; 76% did not receive granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), and prophylaxis was reported in 24% of patients. The most common nonhematologic TEAEs were nausea (57%), fatigue (43%), vomiting (41%), decreased appetite (29%), myalgia (25%), and diarrhea (21%); nonhematologic grade ≥3 events were infrequent (<5%). Progressive disease (PD) was counted as a grade ≥3 TEAE in 17% of patients. The any-grade adjudicated ILD/pneumonitis rate was 6% (7/122), with 1 (0.8%) grade ≥3 event; the median time to first ILD event was 4.6 months (range, 1.3-10.5) after the start of treatment. TEAEs leading to treatment discontinuation occurred in 24 patients (20%), with PD being the reason for 6 (5%); 12/24 patients (10%) discontinued due to treatment-related AEs. TEAEs leading to dose interruption occurred in 72 patients (59%); 41 patients (34%) had a TEAE that led to dose reduction. Treatment-related adverse events led to death in four patients (3%; febrile neutropenia, n = 1 [>3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks]; ILD, n = 1 [3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks]; cardiorespiratory arrest, n = 1 [3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks]; multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, n = 1 [3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks]). In total, 25 patients (20%) had an unrelated TEAE that led to death, the most common of which was disease progression or mCRC in 18 patients (15%).

sec.p: Efficacy data for all patients and by dose level are reported in Table 3. Across all doses, ORR was 15.6% (95% CI, 9.6 to 23.2; 19 confirmed PR), disease control rate was 74.6% (95% CI, 65.9 to 82.0), and DOR was 5.9 months (95% CI, 4.1 to 10.5). Responses were observed across all dose levels but were more frequent at 2.4 mg/kg and 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks (Fig 1). mPFS was 4.6 months (95% CI, 4.0 to 5.4) and mOS was 10.4 months (95% CI, 8.9 to 13.1). Efficacy in patients with known baseline liver metastasis and baseline KRAS mutations are shown in Appendix Table A6. Both 2.4 mg/kg and 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks doses demonstrated antitumor activity; however, 2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks was associated with a higher relative dose intensity and long-term manageable safety compared with 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics
sec.p: At the MTD of 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks, half-lives of Temab-A conjugate and Top1 inhibitor payload adizutecan were 4.7 and 9.3 days, respectively, in the dose escalation and expansion patients with mCRC. Other PK parameters are summarized in Appendix Table A7. The concentration-time profiles for the Temab-A conjugate and the Top1 inhibitor payload are shown in Figure 2. Temab-A conjugate and total antibody concentrations were highly correlated.

sec.title: Exploratory Biomarker Analysis
sec.p: In total, 78 archived samples and 61 recently obtained (within 6 months) tissue samples from patients with mCRC were assessed for c-Met protein expression; 107 patients who had available IHC data in both archival and recently obtained tissue were included, with recently obtained tissue prioritized for the analysis. c-Met protein was expressed across mCRC tissue, with 95% (102/107) of samples demonstrating ≥90% tumor cell staining with ≥1+ intensity and 33 patients (31%) with ≥10% tumor cell staining at strong (IHC staining at 3+) staining intensity. Correlative analysis between target expression and clinical response was performed in all patients excluding those who received the least efficacious dose (1.6 mg/kg once every 3 weeks; n = 1 confirmed response). Patients dosed at ≥2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks were pooled together for the target expression and response correlative analysis. In patients dosed with Temab-A at ≥2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks, ORR was enriched (36.0% [9/25]) in those who had increased c-Met protein expression (≥10%|3+) versus the overall population dosed at ≥2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks (ORR: 20.0% [18/90]); activity was also observed in patients with lower c-Met protein expression (<10%|3+) dosed at Temab-A ≥2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks (ORR, 12.0% [6/50]; Fig 3).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: mCRC remains a challenging disease to treat, particularly in the third-line or later setting, where outcomes remain poor7 and treatment options are limited. In this study, we investigated the hypothesis that the c-Met–targeted ADC Temab-A could be safely administered and induce objective responses in patients with mCRC.

Our data indicate that Temab-A is tolerable, with manageable TEAEs that are consistent with those reported for other Top1 inhibitor ADCs.20,21 Although a high proportion of patients reported grade ≥3 hematologic events, these—and any grade hematologic events—generally did not lead to discontinuation and were managed through dose reductions, interruptions, blood transfusions, or prophylactic G-CSF when clinically indicated. Nonhematologic toxicities included fatigue and nausea, with the majority of GI events (70%) being low-grade. ILD/pneumonitis events were generally low-grade and did not appear to be dose-dependent as they were observed across all dose levels; the only grade ≥3 event occurred at 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks.

Across the dose range of 1.6-3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks, lower doses were associated with lower frequency and severity of hematologic events. During dose escalation, 1 DLT was observed in the 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks dose cohort (n = 18) during backfilling after completion of dose escalation; 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks was selected as the MTD. DLTs were observed at doses >3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks and were primarily hematologic. The 2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks dose exhibited improved tolerability versus the 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks dose, with fewer high-grade hematologic toxicities. Relative dose intensity was also higher at the 2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks versus 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks dose, underscoring the importance of dose optimization in balancing efficacy and safety to identify the most appropriate dose for future development. The totality of safety, efficacy, and PK data, as well as the dose intensity analyses for all three evaluable doses in patients with mCRC, indicate that as a monotherapy, the 2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks dose of Temab-A had a better safety profile versus 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks, while showing meaningful efficacy.

In the context of the third-line or later treatment setting for mCRC, where the results of recent trials such as FRESCO-2 (fruquintinib) and trifluridine/tipiracil plus bevacizumab reported modest survival benefits (mPFS, 3.7-5.6 months and mOS, 7.4-10.8 months),8,9 Temab-A monotherapy demonstrated promising efficacy in heavily pretreated patients. Across all Temab-A doses, the ORR was 15.6% and clinically meaningful activity was observed at doses of 2.4 mg/kg and 3.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks (ORRs of 17.5% and 24.4%, respectively). The mPFS was 5.3 months and mOS was 10.7 months at 2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks. Together with a manageable safety profile, these data support 2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks as the RP2D for further evaluation of Temab-A monotherapy in mCRC.

Biomarker analysis revealed that the ORR was particularly enriched in patients with mCRC who received Temab-A at doses ≥2.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks and had increased c-Met protein expression (≥10%|3+; ORR was 36.0% in patients with IHC results v 20.0% in patients with mCRC who had available tissue). Temab-A also elicited antitumor activity in patients who had lower c-Met protein expression (<10%|3+; ORR of 12.0%). These data validate c-Met protein as a target in mCRC.

The ADC design of Temab-A represents a novel approach to overcoming limitations of other c-Met–targeted therapies. Small molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors of c-Met tend to target tumors that have MET amplification or MET exon 14 skipping mutations and have demonstrated limited efficacy in mCRC,22 potentially due to challenges with achieving selective and sustained inhibition of c-Met signaling in heterogeneous tumors. Conversely, Temab-A is a first-in-class ADC delivering a potent Top1 inhibitor payload directly to c-Met protein–expressing tumor cells. Its design, similar to other ADCs, minimizes damage to healthy cells and reduces systemic toxicity and off-target effects,23,24 as expression of its target c-Met protein is generally lower on healthy cells than the threshold required for ADC-induced cytotoxicity.25 These characteristics distinguish Temab-A from traditional Top1 inhibitors, which have been associated with significant toxicity issues in normal tissue,26-28 and contribute to its favorable activity in the mCRC population.

One potential study limitation was that some patients included in this analysis had c-Met protein expression measured on archival tumor samples, while others' was measured on recently obtained tissue. Additionally, the management of cytopenias was initially left to the discretion of the investigator, and this may have led to variability in the frequency of transfusions and prophylactic G-CSF.

In conclusion, Temab-A monotherapy demonstrated manageable safety and promising antitumor activity in patients with mCRC, addressing a critical unmet need for effective targeted therapies in this population. The enriched responses observed among patients with increased c-Met protein expression reinforce the need for precision medicine to optimize treatment outcomes in patients with mCRC. Our results suggest that Temab-A may represent an important addition to the third-line mCRC treatment landscape in the future. Larger, randomized studies are needed to validate these findings and to fully characterize the impact of Temab-A on key clinical outcomes.
